Repentance is the act of genuinely feeling sorry for something wrong you have done — and, crucially, deciding to change because of it.

Notice that definition has two parts: the feeling and the turning away. Both are essential. If you only feel bad but don't intend to change, that's not repentance. If you change your behavior but feel nothing about what you did wrong, that's not repentance either. True repentance is both happening together.
Breaking it down piece by piece

Repentance has four inner layers, each building on the one before it:

1. Recognition
You first have to honestly see that what you did was wrong. Not making excuses, not blaming others, not telling yourself it wasn't a big deal. You look at your action clearly and admit: "That was wrong. I did that."

2. Remorse
This is the genuine pain, sorrow, or regret you feel about the wrong you committed. It's not just surface-level embarrassment or the discomfort of getting caught. It's a real, inner ache — a sincere sense of "I shouldn't have done that, and I wish I hadn't."

3. Resolution
Here, you make a firm inner decision: "I will not do this again." You turn away from the wrong action — not because you're forced to, but because you genuinely don't want to be the kind of person who does such things. This is the "turning point" in repentance. Many people describe it as a change of direction from the inside.

4. Making amends (when possible)
Repentance often leads naturally to trying to fix the harm you caused — apologizing to someone you hurt, returning something you took, correcting a lie you told. This isn't always possible (some damage can't be fully undone), but the desire to repair things is usually part of genuine repentance.
How repentance differs from words that look similar

These words are neighbors of repentance, but they're not the same thing:

Repentance vs. Regret
Regret is broader and more passive. You can regret eating too much cake, regret missing a flight, or regret a haircut — things that weren't even morally wrong. Repentance, on the other hand, is specifically about moral wrongdoing, and it carries a commitment to change. Regret says, "I wish that hadn't happened." Repentance says, "I was wrong, and I am going to be different."

Repentance vs. Remorse
Remorse is the painful, guilty feeling you experience after doing something wrong. It's one ingredient of repentance — the emotional part — but repentance is bigger. You can feel remorse and still go back to doing the same wrong thing. Repentance takes that remorse and does something with it: it leads to change.

Repentance vs. Guilt
Guilt is also just a feeling — the internal signal that tells you something you did violated your own sense of right and wrong. Guilt can be healthy (it pushes you toward repentance) or it can become unhealthy (when it paralyzes you, keeps you stuck, and leads nowhere). Repentance is what happens when you respond to guilt productively: you face what you did, feel genuine sorrow, and change.

Repentance vs. Apology
An apology is something you say to another person. Repentance is something that happens inside you. You can give an apology without repentance (hollow, insincere words). And you can have deep repentance even without having the chance to apologize yet (perhaps the person is no longer in your life). Apology is an outward act; repentance is an inward transformation.
Where and how this word is used

In religion and spirituality
This is where "repentance" is used most often, and where it carries the deepest weight. In Christianity, Islam, Judaism, and many other traditions, repentance is a central spiritual act — turning away from wrongdoing and returning to God or to one's moral path. It's seen not as a sign of weakness but as one of the most courageous and important things a person can do. Religious teachings often describe repentance as the beginning of healing and renewal.

"The preacher called on his congregation to live lives of sincere repentance."

In everyday moral life
Outside of religious settings, repentance describes the same inner process when someone truly comes to terms with harm they've caused — to another person, to a community, or even to themselves — and commits to doing better.

"After years of hurting people with his anger, there was a quiet but unmistakable repentance in the way he now spoke and acted."

In formal or public contexts
You'll sometimes see it used to describe someone's public acknowledgment of wrongdoing, like a criminal expressing repentance before a court, or a public figure owning up to serious mistakes.

"The judge noted the defendant's evident repentance and took it into account in sentencing."

Understanding what a word doesn't mean is just as important as knowing what it does.

  • Repentance is not just saying "sorry." Words without inner change are hollow. Real repentance is proven over time through behavior, not just declared in a moment.
  • Repentance is not self-punishment. Some people confuse repentance with torturing themselves with guilt endlessly. Genuine repentance acknowledges wrong, feels appropriate sorrow, and then moves forward — it doesn't keep you trapped in self-loathing.
  • Repentance is not weakness. It actually demands tremendous honesty and courage. Admitting you were wrong, facing the harm you caused, and committing to change is one of the harder things a person can do. It's far easier to make excuses or deny wrongdoing.
  • Repentance is not always a single moment. Sometimes it's a gradual process. A person might begin to see that they were wrong, slowly feel the weight of it, and over days or weeks arrive at a genuine change of heart. The word can describe that entire journey.
A simple mental image to hold onto

Think of repentance like realizing you've been walking in the wrong direction.

First, you notice you're going the wrong way (recognition). Then you feel the frustration and regret of the wrong path you've been on (remorse). Then you stop, turn around, and start walking the right way (resolution). And if you've knocked something over while going the wrong direction, you go back and pick it up (making amends).

The key image is the turning around — which is, at heart, what repentance is all about.
Repentance is the genuine, heartfelt acknowledgment that you have done something wrong, accompanied by real sorrow for it and a sincere commitment to change your ways.
